An architectural walk along Wilcza street, with a photograph on page 15 captioned “Hełm w dachu kamienicy przy ul. Wilczej 29” and credited to J.S. Majewski. Accessed 27 August 2026.
sources.title: Jak za dawnych lat
sources.creator: Jerzy S. Majewski
sources.researchNote: The walk explains why this address can still be seen at all: Wilcza was bombed less heavily than the neighbouring streets, escaped the post-war plans for rebuilding the district, and kept a long row of its nineteenth- and early twentieth-century tenements, among them the houses at 25, 28, 30 and 32. The article documents the neighbouring 29A as the work of the practice of Wacław Heppen and Józef Napoleon Czerwiński, and its photograph shows that the roof turret of number 29 survives. What it does not give is a view of the house as Kaper knew it: the picture was taken in 2017 by the author of the article, and the street lost part of its fabric in 1944.

timelineEvents.title: Police certificate records Mosaic religion
timelineEvents.label: Mosaic religion recorded
timelineEvents.shortDescription: A police certificate issued shortly before Kaper’s baptism recorded his religion as “Mosaic,” the official term then used for the Jewish faith.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The certificate of good conduct issued by the Warsaw State Police forms an important documentary link between Kaper’s university records and the later baptismal entry. It anchors the discussion of identity in administrative sources rather than retrospectively imposed narratives: Kaper appears in the record as a young Warsaw student from an assimilated Jewish family whose formal confessional status changed only a few months later.
